At the heart of every meaning of generation is one simple idea: something being brought into existence — whether people, things, or energy — as part of a continuing sequence or cycle. Keep this in mind as you read through each meaning, and you'll notice they all connect back to it.
Meaning 1: A Group of People Born Around the Same Time

This is the most common use of the word.

A generation is a large group of people who were born and grew up during roughly the same period of time. Because they share the same era, they also tend to share similar experiences — the same music, technology, historical events, social values, and challenges. This shared background shapes how they see the world.

"My grandmother belongs to a different generation — she grew up without television or smartphones."

"The younger generation is more comfortable with technology than the older generation."

How long is a generation? Roughly 25 to 30 years. This comes from the biological idea of parents and their children — the time it takes for one set of people to grow up and have children of their own.

Named Generations

Over the decades, researchers and writers have given names to specific generations:

  • The Greatest Generation — born roughly 1901–1927; lived through the Great Depression and World War II
  • The Silent Generation — born roughly 1928–1945
  • Baby Boomers — born roughly 1946–1964; named for the large "boom" in births after World War II
  • Generation X — born roughly 1965–1980
  • Millennials (Generation Y) — born roughly 1981–1996; grew up alongside the rise of the internet
  • Generation Z (Gen Z) — born roughly 1997–2012; the first generation to grow up entirely with smartphones
  • Generation Alpha — born roughly 2013–present; growing up with AI and advanced technology

These names are useful for talking about broad cultural and social trends, but remember: they are generalizations. Not every person within a generation fits the same pattern.

The Generation Gap

When two generations think or behave very differently from each other, we call it a generation gap. This phrase captures the idea that a significant difference — in values, habits, beliefs, or communication styles — has opened up between people of different age groups.

"There's a real generation gap between parents and teenagers when it comes to social media."
Meaning 2: A Single Step in a Family Line

In the context of family and ancestry, a generation is one step in the chain from ancestor to descendant.

Think of it this way: your grandparents are one generation, your parents are the next generation, you are the next, and your children (if you have them) will be the next after that.

"She is the third generation of her family to run this bakery — her grandmother started it, her mother carried it on, and now she runs it."

"This problem has persisted for generations." (meaning: for many decades, passed down through multiple family lines)

First Generation, Second Generation

You'll often hear these phrases when talking about immigrants:

  • First-generation immigrant: Someone who moved to a new country themselves.
  • Second-generation immigrant: Someone born in the new country to parents who immigrated.
  • Third-generation: Grandchildren of the original immigrants, born and raised entirely in the new country.

Each step down the family line is one generation.
Meaning 3: The Act or Process of Producing Something

Here, generation refers to the act of creating or producing something — not a group of people, but a process or output.

"The generation of electricity from solar panels has grown dramatically."

"The generation of new ideas is central to any creative business."

"This machine is responsible for the generation of heat."

In this sense, "generation" is nearly a synonym for production, creation, or output — but it often implies that what is being produced comes from a system or process that keeps running and producing.

Common phrases using this sense:

  • Lead generation (business): The process of finding potential customers.
  • Heat generation: The production of heat by a machine, chemical reaction, or living body.
  • Power generation: Producing electrical power (from coal, wind, solar, etc.).
  • Content generation: Producing written, visual, or audio content — now often associated with AI.
Meaning 4: A Stage in Technological Development

Technology also uses the word generation — borrowed from the family meaning — to describe successive stages of a product or technology, where each new version is an advancement over the previous one.

"The latest generation of smartphones is far more powerful than those from five years ago."

"Fifth-generation (5G) wireless networks offer much faster speeds than 4G."

"Next-generation aircraft are being designed with new fuel efficiency standards."

Just as in a family, where each generation is a "new version" of the one before it, technology generations represent a new version or stage of development — often involving major improvements or a fundamental redesign.
How All These Meanings Are Connected

It helps to see the word as having one underlying logic:

A generation is always about a point in a continuing sequence — a cycle of producing, inheriting, and passing on.

Whether it's:

  • People being born into an era (human generations),
  • Children inheriting from parents (family generations),
  • Electricity being produced (generation of power),
  • Or a new model of a product (technological generation) —

…the word always carries the idea of something coming into being as part of an ongoing process or sequence.

Generation as a noun can mean:

  1. A group of people born in the same era, sharing a common cultural experience (Baby Boomers, Gen Z, etc.)
  2. A single step in a family line — the distance between parents and their children (roughly 25–30 years)
  3. The act of producing or creating something — electricity, ideas, heat, leads, content
  4. A stage in technological or product development — first-generation, next-generation, 5G

• "My parents' generation had very different values from mine." → group of people from an era
  • "This tradition has been passed down for six generations." → steps in a family line
  • "The generation of renewable energy is crucial for the future." → act of producing something
  • "The new generation of electric cars can travel over 500 miles on one charge." → stage in technological development
  • "There's always been a generation gap between teenagers and their grandparents." → cultural difference between age groups
